tasks.task: Look up TRL's forward modelling in the hugging face documentation on how to add a margin to a loss.
tasks.answer: Final Response: According to TRL's Reward Modeling documentation (section 'Adding a margin to the loss', https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/v0.12.2/reward_trainer), to add a margin to the loss you add a 'margin' column to your dataset that stores the difference between the chosen and rejected rewards, e.g. def add_margin(row): return {'margin': row['score_chosen'] - row['score_rejected']} followed by dataset = dataset.map(add_margin). The reward collator automatically passes the margin through and the Bradley-Terry loss is computed accordingly, penalizing examples where the chosen reward does not exceed the rejected reward by at least the margin (as in the Llama 2 paper).

tasks.task: In the Hugging Face documentation, find the tutorial on loading adapters with PEFT, tell me how to load in 8bit or 4bit.
tasks.answer: In the Hugging Face PEFT adapter-loading tutorial (https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/peft), to load an adapter in 8bit or 4bit you use bitsandbytes quantization: create a BitsAndBytesConfig with load_in_8bit=True for 8-bit (or load_in_4bit=True for 4-bit, optionally with bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4") and pass it as quantization_config to AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained / PeftModel.from_pretrained together with device_map="auto". Example (8bit): quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True); model = AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("peft_adapter_path", quantization_config=quantization_config, device_map="auto").

tasks.task: Investigate the 'transformers' library in the Hugging Face documentation, focusing on how to add new tokens to a tokenizer.
tasks.answer: Investigated the Hugging Face transformers documentation on adding new tokens to a tokenizer. Opened https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/index, used the documentation search control with query 'add tokens', and opened the Tokenizer API page (https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v5.20.2/main_classes/tokenizer). Key findings: new regular tokens are added with PreTrainedTokenizer.add_tokens(new_tokens) and special tokens with PreTrainedTokenizer.add_special_tokens(...); tokens already in the vocabulary are not re-added and the method returns the number of tokens actually added. After extending the tokenizer, the model's embedding matrix must be resized with model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer)) so the model can use the new tokens. Verified on-page occurrences: add_tokens=11, add_special_tokens=9, resize_token_embeddings=1.

tasks.task: Investigate in the Hugging Face documentation how to utilize the 'Trainer' API for training a model on a custom dataset, and note the configurable parameters of the Trainer class.
tasks.answer: Final Response: How to utilize the Trainer API for training on a custom dataset (Hugging Face Transformers docs): 1) Prepare the custom dataset and tokenize/preprocess it (e.g., with datasets.load_dataset or your own torch Dataset). 2) Define a TrainingArguments object (the args parameter) holding all training hyperparameters such as learning_rate, num_train_epochs, per_device_train_batch_size, output_dir. 3) Instantiate the trainer: trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, eval_dataset=eval_dataset, data_collator=..., processing_class/tokenizer=..., compute_metrics=...). 4) Launch training with trainer.train() (and evaluate with trainer.evaluate()). Configurable constructor parameters of the Trainer class: model, args, data_collator, train_dataset, eval_dataset, processing_class, model_init, compute_metrics, callbacks, optimizers, preprocess_logits_for_metrics.

tasks.task: Check out Text Embeddings Inference in Hugging face's Doc to summarise the strengths of the toolkit.
tasks.answer: Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) toolkit strengths, summarised from the Hugging Face Docs page (https://huggingface.co/docs/text-embeddings-inference/index): TEI is a blazing fast, production-ready toolkit for serving open-source text embedding models (FlagEmbedding, Ember, GTE, E5). Its key strengths are: (1) streamlined deployment — serve embedding models with a single Docker container on GPU or CPU; (2) efficient resource utilization with optimized, low-latency inference; (3) dynamic batching of requests to maximize throughput; (4) optimized inference backends (e.g., Flash Attention / Candle) for high performance; (5) fast and safe model loading via Safetensors for quicker boot times; (6) production-ready observability with metrics and tracing.
